title: Mechelen incident
summary: Major Erich Hoenmanns became disoriented in low fogbanks during a flight from Loddenheide to Cologne and crossed into Belgium. While circling over Vucht, he accidentally cut the fuel supply to the engine, forcing a forced landing in a field near Maasmechelen. The aircraft was severely damaged when both wings struck Canadian poplar trees, but the pilot and passenger survived uninjured.
probable_cause: Pilot error: became lost in fog, navigated into Belgian airspace, and inadvertently cut fuel supply to the engine.

notes: historical WWII military-diplomatic incident rather than commercial accident

title: Kaleva

location.name: Gulf of Finland near Keri Island

summary: Kaleva, a Finnish civilian Junkers Ju 52 passenger aircraft, was shot down by two Soviet DB-3 torpedo bombers over the Gulf of Finland on June 14, 1940. The incident occurred during the interim peace between Finland and the USSR, immediately before the Soviet occupation of Estonia. All nine passengers and crew were killed; victims' bodies were never recovered.

factors.evidence: Soviet DB-3 torpedo bombers opened fire with machine guns and lethally damaged Kaleva

title: 1940 Canberra air disaster
summary: A Lockheed Hudson aircraft carrying three Australian cabinet ministers stalled during landing approach at Canberra in fine weather and descended into a hill. All 10 occupants were killed instantly in the crash and subsequent fire. The aircraft had been in service only four months with minimal flight time, and evidence suggests a crew member may have been flying.
probable_cause: Aerodynamic stall during landing approach at excessive descent rate resulting in loss of control at altitude too low to recover.

factors.evidence: Aircraft believed to have stalled on its landing approach, when it was too low to recover

Possible that Minister Fairbairn persuaded RAAF crew to allow him to fly the plane into Canberra; question later raised about pilot-in-command Flt Lt Hitchcock's flying ability and whether he was even at the controls

Aircraft burned fiercely after impact, charring bodies of those on board

events.text: Flight Lieutenant Hitchcock and three crew members departed RAAF Laverton for Essendon to pick up passengers

title: Lovettsville air disaster
summary: Pennsylvania Central Airlines Flight 19, a new Douglas DC-3, crashed near Lovettsville, Virginia on August 31, 1940, killing all 25 aboard including U.S. Senator Ernest Lundeen. While flying at 6,000 feet on approach to Pittsburgh, the aircraft encountered an intense thunderstorm near the West Virginia border. Witnesses reported seeing a large flash of lightning shortly before the aircraft nosed over and plunged to earth in an alfalfa field with wreckage scattered over a broad area.
probable_cause: Lightning strike encountered during flight through intense thunderstorm near Lovettsville, Virginia caused loss of control and structural failure.

title: 1940 Brocklesby mid-air collision
operator: No. 2 Service Flying Training School RAAF
summary: Two Avro Ansons operated by No. 2 Service Flying Training School collided at 300 meters altitude over Brocklesby on 29 September 1940. Leading Aircraftman Fuller in N4876 lost sight of Hewson's aircraft during a banking turn. The aircraft collided and became mechanically locked with the lower Anson's turret wedged into the upper wing root. The upper aircraft's engines stopped but the lower aircraft's engines continued running. Fuller successfully controlled the locked aircraft and made an emergency belly landing. All four crew survived.
probable_cause: Loss of situational awareness by the upper aircraft pilot who failed to maintain visual contact with the other aircraft during a banking turn at low altitude during training.

factors.evidence: Fuller lost sight of Hewson's aircraft beneath him

events.text: Both aircraft at 300 m altitude over the township of Brocklesby making a banking turn.
The Ansons collided with a grinding crash and roaring propellers struck engine cowlings.
Both of the upper aircraft's engines had been knocked out but those below continued at full power.
Fuller found he was able to control the interlocked Ansons with his ailerons and flaps.
The two navigators and the lower Anson's pilot bailed out of the aircraft.
Fuller travelled 8 km and successfully made an emergency belly landing in a large paddock.
The locked aircraft slid 200 yards across grass before coming to rest.

notes: All four crew survived despite severe collision
Upper Anson returned to flight service after repair

title: 1940 Deutsche Lufthansa Ju 90 crash
summary: The Junkers Ju 90 Brandenburg took off from Berlin Tempelhof Airport at 14:24 on 8 November 1940 with 29 people on board. Radio contact at 14:48 reported flying at 2,200 metres in clouds with icing conditions. Two minutes later the final call was made and the aircraft descended uncontrollably. Investigation found ice accumulation exceeding 1.5 inches thick had jammed the elevator controls, causing loss of altitude from 2,200 metres to ground level in three to five minutes.
probable_cause: ice accumulation on flight surfaces exceeding 1.5 inches thickness jammed elevator controls leading to uncontrolled loss of altitude

factors.evidence: ice was found on the aircraft that was more than 1.5 inches thick

events.text: The aircraft took off from Berlin Tempelhof Airport at 14:24
